subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: pausing to reset after a conflict over guests [Revision]
passage: Pradeep, you look tense about your guest list, so let me tell you what my husband and I did. I'm Shreya. Ten days before our wedding we had a shouting match over it. He wanted a hundred and fifty, and I had found myself adding relatives until it reached three hundred. I walked out to the balcony, he stayed in the kitchen, and we didn't speak for an hour. Then he came out with two cups of tea. We set a cap of two hundred and a rule: exceptions only if both of us agreed. The next day we sat with each set of parents and said why: "We want to be able to talk with everyone who comes." Both families listened. It hurt less because we had both stopped fighting first.

qa.q: What cap did the couple set for the guests?
qa.a: They set a cap of two hundred.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel on walking out to the balcony?
qa.a: Shreya was upset and frustrated after the shouting match, and needed a pause before speaking again.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped end the fight, and why?
qa.a: Stopping for an hour and then agreeing a cap with a rule for exceptions helped, because it replaced arguing about numbers with a shared limit.

qa.q: How might Shreya's husband have felt when he brought out the two cups of tea?
qa.a: He probably felt regret and a wish to make peace, offering tea as a way to reopen the conversation.

grounding: Illustrates a couple stepping back after a heated fight over the guest list, agreeing a cap and a rule for exceptions and explaining it kindly to both families.

The printer needed the final guest count by nine the next morning, and at eleven at night Ishita and Karthik were shouting in the kitchen of their rented flat in Chennai.
"Your mother added thirty people today!"
"And your father added twenty-five last week!"
Karthik slammed the list on the counter. Then he stopped, breathed, and sat on the floor. "This isn't working."
Ishita sat next to him. After a minute, she said, "Let's stop adding and make a rule. A cap. Two hundred and fifty."
"And exceptions?"
"Only if someone we'd actually miss would be hurt. And we both have to agree."
They went through the list quietly with that rule. Two exceptions made it; the rest didn't.
At midnight they wrote a message to both families: the cap, the reason (the hall size and their savings), and a thank-you. They sent the count to the printer at eight fifty.

qa.q: What was the guest cap Ishita suggested?
What was Karthik feeling when he sat down on the floor?
qa.a: He was frustrated and exhausted from the fight, and stepping back showed he wanted to stop hurting each other.

qa.q: What else could the couple have done if the families had objected to the message?
qa.a: They could have called each family, listened to their concerns, and explained the rule again with the same kind reasons.

qa.q: How might Karthik's mother see the couple's message?
qa.a: She may feel disappointed that some of her thirty names were cut, but a clear reason and a thank-you make it easier to accept.

grounding: It shows a couple, after a heated fight over guests, stepping back to agree a cap and an exception rule and explaining it kindly to both families under deadline.

subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations

passage:
The fight in Darshan and Aditi's Pune flat started over a single name: Aditi's college friend's parents.
"You don't even know them!"
"You invited your entire gym!"
Aditi grabbed her keys and walked out. Darshan sat on the balcony, angry and then just tired.
She came back an hour later with two cups of tea. "Can we start again? Not the list. The rules."
They agreed on a cap of two hundred. Then an exception rule: someone outside the cap comes only if both of them would feel the person's absence at the wedding. Not one, both.
Suddenly the list was easy. The gym friends were out. The college friend's parents, who had once fed Aditi for a month, were in; Darshan agreed after hearing that.
On Sunday they visited both sets of parents together and explained: the cap, the rule, the reasons. Aditi's mother grumbled, then said, "Fine. At least it's fair."

qa.q: What was the cap Darshan and Aditi agreed on?
How did Darshan feel on the balcony after Aditi walked out?
qa.a: Darshan felt angry at first, then just tired and drained by the fight.

qa.q: What else could the couple do if new requests arrived after the list was sent?
qa.a: They could apply the same exception rule to each request, and explain it kindly each time rather than reopening the whole list.

qa.q: How might Aditi's mother see the new rule?
qa.a: Aditi's mother grumbled at first but found the rule fair, which made it easier to accept even without every name she wanted.

grounding: It shows a couple stepping back after a fight over guests, agreeing a cap and an exception rule, and explaining it to both families with reasons.
